paragraphs: Zuga of Adiabene. See above, Yaakov of Adiabene: it is a place name. The Arukh, entry Hadyav, likewise says so. Rav Huna (see his entry) died …; Zuga of Adiabene taught them. See Arukh, entry Chadyav: in chapter Asarah Yuchasin, 72, “Chavor is Chadyav”; the Targum renders Ashkenaz as Chadyav (see there). In Arukh, entry Zava, at the end of the Gemara Mashkin—a marginal note says folio 10, but it is not there, rather Moed Katan chapter 3, 28a—“Zava of Adiabene taught them.” In Niddah 21b, “Zava of Adiabene came, bringing a teaching”; it explains: the name of a sage. End of Arukh. Our reading in Moed Katan and Niddah is Zuga; Rashi in Niddah and in Ein Yaakov’s Moed Katan explains: two Torah scholars. Likewise Sanhedrin 12a: they sent Rava, “A pair came from Rakkat”; Rashi: two Torah scholars came from Rakkat, Tiberias. See Arukh, entry zav: it brings many places where zava means two. In all the places Arukh brings, our Talmud has zuga for his zava. It appears as Arukh explains, that Zava or Zuga is a sage’s name, not an expression for two, because it says tana lehu Zuga—or Zava, Arukh’s reading—where it should have said tanu lehu in the plural. Therefore Niddah says ata veayti, “he came and brought,” not atu, “they came.” See shortly below, where Zuga is a sage’s name. In Jerusalem Talmud, Megallechin,end of halakhah 1, a pair came before Rava concerning the moustache and cutting nails, and he permitted them. Rabbi Simon in Rabbi Chanina’s name: there were two pairs, one from Ammetan and one from Middad; one concerning the moustache, one concerning cutting nails …. Here it appears to mean two.
